prompt.provenance_instruction: Answer the following question about Drosophila neuroscience. For every claim you make, state where the information comes from - for example: the specific database, dataset, or tool query you used; the publication (with full citation); or your general training knowledge. If you are uncertain or do not have a source, say so explicitly rather than guessing.

results.title: Brain region identification
results.question: What are the major subdivisions of the Drosophila mushroom body?
results.response: The major subdivisions of the [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005801 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain") are the calyx, pedunculus, and mushroom body lobe system. The calyx is closest to the cortex and receives sensory interneuron afferents. The pedunculus is a thick axon bundle extending from the calyx to the base of the lobes. The mushroom body lobe system consists of a vertical branch and a medial branch, which have different structures at different life stages.

results.title: Neuron type classification
results.question: What types of Kenyon cells exist in the adult Drosophila brain?
results.response: There are multiple types of Kenyon cells in the adult Drosophila brain, including [KCab-c(i)](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00049111 "Open KCab-c(i) in Virtual Fly Brain"), [KCab-c](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00110929 "Open KCab-c in Virtual Fly Brain"), [KCg-m](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00111061 "Open KCg-m in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Kenyon cell of main calyx](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047926 "Open Kenyon cell of main calyx in Virtual Fly Brain"), and [gamma Kenyon cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00100247 "Open gamma Kenyon cell in Virtual Fly Brain"). Additionally, Kenyon cells can be classified into alpha/beta, alpha'/beta', and gamma Kenyon cells, which are further subdivided into subtypes such as core/surface/posterior, anterior-posterior/middle, and dorsal/main/gamma-s/gamma-t classes. VFB holds [37](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003686,SubclassesOf "Run in VFB: Subclasses of Kenyon cell") subclasses of [Kenyon cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003686 "Open Kenyon cell in Virtual Fly Brain").

results.response: The main input neurons to the [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005801 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain") are projection neurons from the antennal lobe and sensory interneuron afferents to the calyx.

results.title: Gene expression
results.question: What neurotransmitter do mushroom body Kenyon cells use?
results.response: The primary neurotransmitter used by mushroom body Kenyon cells, such as alpha/beta core Kenyon cells, is acetylcholine. VFB records show that Kenyon cells are cholinergic, i.e. they use acetylcholine.

results.title: Cell count
results.question: Approximately how many neurons are in the adult Drosophila central brain?
results.response:
The number of neurons is approximately more than 125,000.

**Published neuron-count estimates — adult central brain** (from the literature):

- more than 125,000 neurons (adult Drosophila central brain connectome/model) — A Drosophila computational brain model reveals sensorimotor processing. — PMID 39358519
- ~139,255 neurons (whole adult Drosophila brain) — Neuronal wiring diagram of an adult brain. — PMID 39358518

_VFB has annotated 9,413 neuron types with some part in adult central brain — a curated annotation count, not the biological total._

results.title: Central complex structure
results.question: What are the main components of the Drosophila central complex and what functions are they associated with?
results.response: The main components of the central complex include the ellipsoid body, the fan-shaped body, the paired noduli, the asymmetrical bodies, and the protocerebral bridge. These components are associated with functions such as navigation/orientation, locomotor control, and sleep/arousal or memory-related behaviours.

results.title: Genetic tools
results.question: What genetic tools are commonly used to label mushroom body neurons in Drosophila?
results.response: Genetic tools such as PBac{544.SVS-1}Bsg[CPTI100062], PBac{566.P.SVS-1}Bsg[CPTI100005], and PBac{602.P.SVS-1}Fas2[CPTI000483] are used to label neurons. Kenyon cells are a type of neuron in the mushroom bodies of Drosophila. VFB does not currently hold data on which specific genetic tools are commonly used to label mushroom body neurons, including Kenyon cells.

results.title: Circuit motif
results.question: Describe the dopaminergic input to mushroom body output neurons (MBONs). Which DAN types connect to which MBON types?
results.response: Dopaminergic input to mushroom body output neurons comes from specific types of dopaminergic neurons. The dopaminergic PPL1 neuron provides input to the adult [mushroom body output neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047953 "Open mushroom body output neuron in Virtual Fly Brain"). Additionally, the dopaminergic PAM neuron 6 is also a source of dopaminergic input to mushroom body output neurons. The connectivity data indicates that there are specific pairs of dopaminergic neurons and mushroom body output neurons that are connected, such as the dopaminergic PPL1 neuron and the adult mushroom body output neuron. VFB has annotated 84 upstream class-connectivity partners matching "dopaminergic neuron" for mushroom body output neurons. The question of which specific DAN types connect to which MBON types is not fully answered by the available data, as the term "DAN types" is not clearly defined in this context.

results.title: Neuron characterisation
results.question: What is known about the LPLC2 visual neuron type? Where is it, what does it connect to, and what is its function?
results.response: The [lobula plate-lobula columnar neuron LPLC2](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00111763 "Open lobula plate-lobula columnar neuron LPLC2 in Virtual Fly Brain") is located in the dorsal area of the lateral cell body rind and has distinct dendritic arbors in each lobula plate layer. This arrangement allows it to detect looming stimuli, and its activity elicits a jump escape response. In the lobula, it has its main dendritic arbors in layers 4 and 5B, with minor processes in layer 5A, and presynaptic sites in layer 4. The arbors of LPLC2 span approximately 25 lobula optic columns, overlapping with other LPLC2 cells. LPLC2 projects to an optic glomerulus of the PVLP, anterior to LPLC1 and dorsal to LC4. There are approximately 80 of these cells per optic lobe, and they are cholinergic.

results.title: Comparative anatomy
results.question: How does the organisation of the antennal lobe compare between adult and larval Drosophila?
results.response: The organisation of the [antennal lobe](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003924 "Open antennal lobe in Virtual Fly Brain") compares between adult and larval Drosophila in terms of glomerular organization. Both stages are glomerular, but the adult antennal lobe is represented as the more elaborated glomerular neuropil. VFB does not currently hold data on other aspects of the comparison.

results.title: Publications for a circuit
results.question: What publications describe the PPL1 dopaminergic neurons and their role in aversive memory?
results.response: Publications describing the dopaminergic PPL1 neurons and their role in aversive memory include Claridge-Chang et al., 2009, Mao and Davis, 2009, Budnik and White, 1988, and Ren et al., 2016.

results.question: Are there neurons in the Hemibrain dataset that are morphologically similar to the fru+ mAL neurons described in light microscopy studies?
results.response: The Hemibrain dataset contains neurons morphologically similar to the fru+ mAL neurons described in light microscopy studies. Neurons with similar morphology include the adult fruitless mAL neuron, adult fru-mAL neuron, fru-aDT-b, and adult fruitless aDT2 neuron.

results.question: Are there reciprocal connections between mushroom body output neurons (MBONs) and dopaminergic neurons (DANs)? Which pairs have the strongest mutual connectivity?
results.response: There are reciprocal connections between mushroom body output neurons and dopaminergic neurons. VFB found 5 reciprocal class-level pairs between these two neuron types. The strongest mutual connectivity is not specified, but the top partners include dopaminergic neurons. The target to source weight pairwise connections are 35.

results.title: Pathway tracing
results.question: Trace a pathway from olfactory receptor neurons to the lateral horn. What are the intermediate neuron types and their connections?
results.response: A pathway from olfactory receptor neurons to the lateral horn involves intermediate neurons, specifically antennal lobe projection neurons. These neurons connect olfactory receptor neurons to the lateral horn. VFB does not currently hold data on other intermediate neuron types in this pathway.

results.response: The [alpha/beta Kenyon cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00100248 "Open alpha/beta Kenyon cell in Virtual Fly Brain") and [gamma Kenyon cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00100247 "Open gamma Kenyon cell in Virtual Fly Brain") have some overlap in their downstream targets. results.title: Anatomical containment chain
results.question: Trace the anatomical containment hierarchy from the DA1 glomerulus up to the top-level brain structure. What is each level in the hierarchy?
results.response: The anatomical containment hierarchy from the DA1 glomerulus up to the top-level brain structure is: DA1 glomerulus -> adult olfactory antennal lobe glomerulus -> adult antennal lobe -> adult deutocerebrum -> adult cerebrum -> adult central brain -> adult brain. VFB does not currently hold data on any other levels in this hierarchy beyond what is listed here.

results.response: Neurons that connect the [adult central complex](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003632 "Open adult central complex in Virtual Fly Brain") to the [lateral accessory lobe on L3 CNS template, Wood2018](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFB_00050314 "Open lateral accessory lobe on L3 CNS template, Wood2018 in Virtual Fly Brain") include [PFL1](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00111433 "Open PFL1 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [PFL2_PB4](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00111453 "Open PFL2_PB4 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [PFL3_PB7](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00111450 "Open PFL3_PB7 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [PFL1_PB1](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00111434 "Open PFL1_PB1 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [PFL1_PB7](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00111440 "Open PFL1_PB7 in Virtual Fly Brain"), and [PFL1_PB2](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00111435 "Open PFL1_PB2 in Virtual Fly Brain"). results.question: For the DNa02 descending neuron type, what data is available in VFB? Is it in the Hemibrain, FAFB, or both? Are there light microscopy images and driver lines?
results.response: Data for [descending neuron of the anterior dorsal brain DNa02](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047573 "Open descending neuron of the anterior dorsal brain DNa02 in Virtual Fly Brain") is available, including light microscopy images and driver lines. There are [18](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047573,ListAllAvailableImages "Run in VFB: List all available images of DNa02") images available. Downstream connectivity classes for DNa02 include [636](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047573,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for DNa02") downstream neuron classes, and upstream connectivity classes include [779](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047573,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for DNa02") upstream neuron classes. Genetic tools are available to label DNa02 descending neurons. VFB does not currently hold data on whether DNa02 is in the Hemibrain or FAFB, or both.

results.title: Complete neuron profile
results.question: Give me a comprehensive profile of the giant fiber neuron: its anatomy, connectivity, available driver lines, and relevant publications.
results.response:
The [giant fiber neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00004020 "Open giant fiber neuron in Virtual Fly Brain") is a large adult descending neuron that controls jump escape behavior. It can be identified by its large descending axon, which is several times larger than any other axon in the cervical connective. The giant fiber neuron has dendritic arborization in the ipsilateral zones A and B of the antennal mechanosensory and motor center. 

The giant fiber neuron is connected to various neurons, including adult VNC neurons, thoracic neurons, secondary neurons, and primary neurons. 

Available driver lines for the giant fiber neuron include [14](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,TransgeneExpressionHere "Run in VFB: Transgene expression in DNp01") transgene expression reports, such as [P{R48A11-GAL4.DBD} ∩ P{R30C01-p65.AD} expression pattern](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFBexp_FBtp0121835FBtp0118557 "Open P{R48A11-GAL4.DBD} ∩ P{R30C01-p65.AD} expression pattern in Virtual Fly Brain") and [P{R68A06-GAL4.DBD} ∩ P{R25C08-p65.AD} expression pattern](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFBexp_FBtp0116198FBtp0118471 "Open P{R68A06-GAL4.DBD} ∩ P{R25C08-p65.AD} expression pattern in Virtual Fly Brain"). 

Relevant publications on the giant fiber neuron include Thomas and Wyman (1984), Koto et al. (1981), Power (1948), Allen et al. (1998), Dorkenwald et al. (2024), and Schlegel et al. (2024). VFB holds 14 records of transgene expression reports for the giant fiber neuron.

results.title: Hypothesis generation
results.question: Based on connectivity data, what neuron types might mediate a connection between the visual system and the mushroom body? Could visual information reach the memory circuit?
results.response: Neuron types that might mediate a connection between the visual system and the [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005801 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain") include projection neurons and visual projection neurons. Adult visual projection neurons to the mushroom body have presynaptic terminals in the mushroom body. This suggests that visual information could reach the memory circuit via these neuron types. VFB does not currently hold data on other specific neuron types that might be involved in this connection.

results.title: Novel circuit exploration
results.question: What is the connectivity between thermosensory neurons and the mushroom body? Could temperature information influence memory formation?
results.response: VFB does not currently hold data on the direct connectivity between thermosensory neurons and the [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005801 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain"). However, VFB holds data on upstream and downstream connectivity classes for [thermosensory neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005918 "Open thermosensory neuron in Virtual Fly Brain"), as well as neurons with some part in mushroom body, which could be used to investigate potential connections. The mushroom body is known to be involved in memory formation, and if thermosensory neurons do connect to it, either directly or indirectly, it is possible that temperature information could influence memory formation. VFB has annotated numerous neurons with parts in the mushroom body and holds images of these neurons, which may be useful for further analysis.

results.title: Data availability survey
results.question: I'm interested in studying the subesophageal zone (SEZ). How well-characterised is this region in VFB? What neuron types are annotated, what connectomics data is available, and what genetic tools exist for SEZ neurons?
results.response: The [subesophageal zone](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00051068 "Open subesophageal zone in Virtual Fly Brain") is characterised with available imagery. VFB holds [4205](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00051068,TransgeneExpressionHere "Run in VFB: Transgene expression in subesophageal zone") genetic tool/expression pattern records for the subesophageal zone, including GAL4 drivers and binary/intersectional drivers. Examples of these genetic tools include [P{GMR12D05-GAL4} expression pattern](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFBexp_FBtp0057511 "Open P{GMR12D05-GAL4} expression pattern in Virtual Fly Brain"), [P{GMR16C05-GAL4} expression pattern](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFBexp_FBtp0057869 "Open P{GMR16C05-GAL4} expression pattern in Virtual Fly Brain"), and P{VT000003-GAL4} expression pattern. VFB does not currently hold data on the specific neuron types annotated in the subesophageal zone or the available connectomics data for this region.

results.response: The [medulla](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003748 "Open medulla in Virtual Fly Brain") has connections via tracts/nerves innervating it, as well as neurons with presynaptic and postsynaptic terminals within it. Neurons with some part in the medulla, and those with synaptic terminals in the medulla, also contribute to its connectivity. The medulla's parts and subclasses, and transgene expression in the medulla, may also be relevant to understanding its connectivity. VFB does not currently hold data on a class-level summary of the medulla's connectivity in graph form.

results.title: Project identity
results.question: What is Virtual Fly Brain and who is it for?
results.response: Virtual Fly Brain is an interactive tool for neurobiologists to explore the detailed neuroanatomy, neuron connectivity, and gene expression of Drosophila melanogaster.

results.title: Citation
results.question: How should I cite Virtual Fly Brain in a publication?
results.response:
To cite Virtual Fly Brain in a publication, use the following citation formats:

```
@article{Court_2023,
author = {Robert Court and Marta Costa and Clare Pilgrim and Gillian Millburn and Alex Holmes and Alex McLachlan and Aoife Larkin and Nicolas Matentzoglu and Huseyin Kir and Helen Parkinson and Nicolas H. Brown and Cahir J. O'Kane and J. Douglas Armstrong and Gregory S. X. E. Jefferis and David Osumi-Sutherland},
title = "{Virtual Fly Brain—An interactive atlas of the Drosophila nervous system}",
journal = {Frontiers in Physiology},
volume = {14},
publisher = {Frontiers Media {SA}},
year = {2023},
month = {jan},
abstract = "{As a model organism, Drosophila is uniquely placed to contribute to our understanding of how brains control complex behavior. Not only does it have complex adaptive behaviors, but also a uniquely powerful genetic toolkit, increasingly complete dense connectomic maps of the central nervous system and a rapidly growing set of transcriptomic profiles of cell types. But this also poses a challenge: Given the massive amounts of available data, how are researchers to Find, Access, Integrate and Reuse (FAIR) relevant data in order to develop an integrated anatomical and molecular picture of circuits, inform hypothesis generation, and find reagents for experiments to test these hypotheses? The Virtual Fly Brain (virtualflybrain.org) web application & API provide a solution to this problem, using FAIR principles to integrate 3D images of neurons and brain regions, connectomics, transcriptomics and reagent expression data covering the whole CNS in both larva and adult. Users can search for neurons, neuroanatomy and reagents by name, location, or connectivity, via text search, clicking on 3D images, search-by-image, and queries by type (e.g., dopaminergic neuron) or properties (e.g., synaptic input in the antennal lobe). Returned results include cross-registered 3D images that can be explored in linked 2D and 3D browsers or downloaded under open licenses, and extensive descriptions of cell types and regions curated from the literature. These solutions are potentially extensible to cover similar atlasing and data integration challenges in vertebrates.}",
issn = {1664-042X},
doi = {10.3389/fphys.2023.1076533},
url = {https://doi.org/10.3389/fphys.2023.1076533},
}
```

Alternatively, you can use the APA, MLA, or Chicago formats:

E., & Osumi-Sutherland, D. (2023). Virtual Fly Brain—An interactive atlas of the Drosophila nervous system. Frontiers in Physiology, 14. https://doi.org/10.3389/fphys.2023.1076533

MLA:

results.title: Concepts: NBLAST
results.question: What is NBLAST and what does an NBLAST similarity score mean?
results.response:
NBLAST is a method used to calculate similarity scores, which represent the morphological similarity between neurons or expression patterns. An NBLAST similarity score is a measure of how similar one neuron or expression pattern is to another. 

The similarity scores are calculated using NBLAST. 

To understand the meaning of an NBLAST similarity score, consider that it is a scored comparison of individual neurons, computed per registered neuron.

To install and get started with VFB-connect in Python, ensure you have Python version 3.10.14, then install the VFBConnect library using

```
pip install vfb-connect
```
and import it using

results.title: API: REST endpoints
results.question: How can I query Virtual Fly Brain programmatically using the SOLR or Owlery API?
results.response: To query Virtual Fly Brain programmatically, you can use the Owlery API, which provides OWL reasoning services for Virtual Fly Brain's ontologies. The API endpoint is https://owl.virtualflybrain.org/ and it enables Description Logic queries, SPARQL queries with OWL reasoning, and access to multiple knowledgebases. Alternatively, the SOLR Search API provides fast text search and autocomplete functionality for Virtual Fly Brain entities, datasets, and publications.

results.title: API: integrations
results.question: How do I explore Virtual Fly Brain neurons using Navis or pymaid?
results.response:
To explore Virtual Fly Brain neurons, you can use the pymaid library to connect to the VFB CATMAID server and retrieve neurons based on their ID or annotations. You can then use navis to plot the neurons. 
```python
import pymaid
import navis

navis.set_pbars(jupyter=False)
pymaid.set_pbars(jupyter=False)

# Connect to the VFB CATMAID server hosting the FAFB data
rm = pymaid.connect_catmaid(server="https://fafb.catmaid.virtualflybrain.org/", api_token=None, max_threads=10)

# Test call to see if connection works 
print(f'Server is running CATMAID version {rm.catmaid_version}')
```
VFB's documentation does not appear to cover Navis. 
VFB's documentation does not appear to cover pymaid.

results.question: Where can I access the FAFB or FANC CATMAID datasets via Virtual Fly Brain?
results.response:
The FAFB CATMAID dataset can be accessed via Virtual Fly Brain. Virtual Fly Brain hosts several CATMAID instances for exploring connectomic reconstruction data, including the VFB CATMAID Adult Brain, which is also known as FAFB.

results.title: Anatomy teaching diagrams
results.question: Is there a circuit diagram of the mushroom body available on Virtual Fly Brain?
results.response: There is a schematic representation of the [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005801 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain") available on Virtual Fly Brain, showing the compartmental organisation of the [adult mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003684 "Open adult mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain") lobes, including how the dendrites of mushroom body output neurons and the axon terminals of dopaminergic neurons tile the lobes into a stereotyped grid of 15 compartments.
